title: Systems concepts: make your boundary inspectable
focus: Construct and challenge two systems-of-interest descriptions without confusing your model with the situation.
scope: A first rehearsal of boundaries, relationships, perspectives, feedback and emergence. It is not a complete treatment of systems philosophy or complexity science.
scenario: Fictional case: Riverbank Library has a computer-booking service. Staff count a booking as successful when a slot is allocated. In one week 80 slots are allocated, 30 are not used, and 20 visitors leave without completing the online application they came to make. The booking form is online. A community group helps people who cannot use it; this work is absent from the library's statistics. Managers propose reducing staff assistance to allocate more slots. Staff predict that visitors will return repeatedly for help. Neither prediction has yet been tested.

rounds.task: Draw an OU-style systems map for the booking manager's system of interest.
rounds.output: A titled containment map with one stated purpose and boundary.
rounds.answer: One defensible title is 'Allocating computer slots'. Within its boundary place the booking process, slot records and allocation staff; put visitors, the community group and application websites in the environment. Containment means inclusion, not causation or seniority. This boundary can be useful for allocation work, but it excludes whether a visitor completes an application. Explain that exclusion rather than pretending the map covers the whole situation.

rounds.task: Construct a second map from a visitor's purpose.
rounds.output: A second boundary and a short explanation of what changed.
rounds.answer: A visitor may define the activity as 'Getting an application completed'. Include access to equipment, assistance, credentials, information and the application process. The library is now one contributor, not the centre of the universe. Include the community group's work. Different maps need not be merged into one allegedly objective map: their purposes differ.

rounds.task: Write a testable feedback hypothesis about reduced assistance.
rounds.output: One closed causal sentence and one observation that could challenge it.
rounds.answer: Less assistance may increase incomplete applications, which may increase repeat visits, which may consume assistance time and further reduce available assistance. This is a proposed reinforcing loop, not a fact established by the numbers. Compare repeat visits and assistance time before and during a small reversible change. A fall in repeats despite reduced assistance would challenge the proposed mechanism.

rounds.task: Locate yourself in the inquiry.
rounds.output: A two-sentence observer note.
rounds.answer: For example: 'I selected completed applications as important because I am taking the visitor's purpose seriously. My questions and reporting may make staff prioritise that measure, so I will ask who loses access or becomes invisible under this new boundary.' Naming the observer does not make every account equally adequate; each still needs evidence and a stated use.

checks.q: Does 80 allocated slots establish 80 successful visitor outcomes?
options: Yes: an output is an outcome
No: allocation and completion are different observations
No: all 80 bookings failed
checks.explanation: Allocation is an output. The case does not establish 80 completed applications, nor does it establish that all bookings failed. The figures may overlap; do not subtract them as though they were disjoint categories.

checks.q: What does a boundary in an OU systems map primarily show?
options: A causal influence
An editorial inclusion in a stated system of interest
A manager's authority
checks.explanation: Containment identifies inclusion at the chosen level. Causal influence and authority require other representations or explicit additional notation.

checks.q: Which observation supports emergence without claiming magic?
options: Repeated local booking decisions can generate an access pattern nobody intended
Every large organisation is unpredictable in every respect
A whole has no relationship to its parts
checks.explanation: An aggregate pattern can arise through interactions rather than anyone designing it. That does not imply universal unpredictability or the irrelevance of components.

repair.broken: The map places every organisation in one circle labelled 'the whole system' and claims that everyone shares the library's success measure.
repair.fix: Give the map a purpose, author, boundary and date. Distinguish an allocation perspective from an application-completion perspective. Record disagreement and missing information. 'Whole' is a claim to examine, not a label that removes the boundary problem.

retry.task: A new manager counts only applications completed on library computers. What exclusion could this introduce, and how would you test it?
retry.answer: People who complete applications later at home or with the community group disappear from the outcome measure. So may people prevented from attending. Ask a sample of visitors about later completion and contact the community group with permission. Do not solve the exclusion merely by broadening a diagram without changing how evidence is collected.

criteria: Each map has a purpose and an explicit boundary.
Containment and causal links are not conflated.
Observed facts, interpretations and predictions are distinguished.
The observer's choices and an excluded perspective are named.

title: Systems laws: test variety, feedback and local optimisation
focus: Use a small disturbance-response model to test a claim about regulation.
scope: Basic examples of requisite variety, feedback delay and whole-system effects. The SCiO row is broader; this page does not claim to cover every law in a systems-laws course.
scenario: Fictional case: a help desk receives four mutually exclusive request states: A password reset, B identity discrepancy, C accessibility support and D suspected fraud. Its safe responses are R1 an automated reset for A, R2 a trained identity investigation for B, R3 supported access for C and R4 a fraud investigation for D. Applying any other response to a state leaves an unacceptable outcome in this deliberately simplified exercise. The new portal can recognise only 'ordinary' and 'exceptional', and offers only R1 or 'send an email'. Replies to that email take five working days. Managers propose counting cases closed by the portal as success.

rounds.task: Construct the disturbance-response table.
rounds.output: Four rows showing the necessary distinction, safe response and current gap.
rounds.answer: A requires R1 and is handled. B requires R2, C requires R3 and D requires R4; the portal's email route does not itself supply those responses. Four labels alone do not solve the problem: recognition, authority, capability and timeliness must support the matching action. In this toy case the safe-response sets are disjoint, so a regulator restricted to two effective responses cannot meet all four requirements.

rounds.task: Design one legitimate attenuation and one amplification.
rounds.output: Two changes, each explaining what variety is changed.
rounds.answer: An authorised upstream identity correction could prevent some B discrepancies arising: it changes the disturbance reaching the desk. Training and authorising an adviser to distinguish B, C and D and route them immediately increases effective response variety. Hiding fraud or accessibility requests from the report merely suppresses information; it does not attenuate the underlying need safely.

rounds.task: Test the five-day feedback delay.
rounds.output: A failure mechanism and an observable warning signal.
rounds.answer: People may resubmit while waiting, increasing workload before the original exception is resolved. Track unique people, repeated submissions, waiting age and unresolved risk, not just portal closures. A lagged weekly total can look reassuring while urgent exceptions accumulate. More frequent reporting helps only if someone can act on the signal.

rounds.task: Replace the local success claim with a test of the whole service.
rounds.output: One outcome measure and one counter-measure.
rounds.answer: Measure safe resolution of the person's request end to end, with unresolved age and access exclusions as counter-measures. Portal closures may be retained as an operational count, but cannot substitute for resolution. The chosen definition of 'safe' and who can contest it must remain explicit.

checks.q: Under this case's disjoint-response assumption, how many distinguishable effective responses are required?
options: Two, because there are two portal labels
Four
An unlimited number
checks.explanation: Four states require four different safe responses in this constructed model. This is not a universal rule that four categories always require four employees or channels.

checks.q: Which proposal changes the disturbance rather than merely hiding it?
options: Exclude inaccessible requests from the dashboard
Correct a recurring upstream identity-record defect
Rename all exceptions 'ordinary'
checks.explanation: Correcting the defect can reduce actual discrepancies. Exclusion and relabelling alter the representation while leaving the need or risk.

checks.q: Can a daily dashboard compensate for an adviser with no authority to act?
options: Yes, information alone supplies control
No, sensing and effective action are both needed
Yes, provided it contains more indicators
checks.explanation: Observation without an available, timely response does not regulate the disturbance. More indicators may instead overload the recipient.

repair.broken: 'The law of requisite variety proves that every customer needs a unique process and standardisation is always wrong.'
repair.fix: The law concerns necessary distinctions and effective regulation relative to desired outcomes. Several disturbances may share an adequate response. Standardise where differences do not matter to that outcome; preserve distinctions and discretion where they do. State the equivalence assumption and test it.

retry.task: B and D can now be safely handled by the same authorised investigation team using one triage action. Does the four-response conclusion still follow?
retry.answer: No. The original disjoint-response assumption has changed. Three initial response classes may suffice if the investigation route actually distinguishes and handles the later differences in time. Count effective response capability across the relevant process, not merely the first screen's buttons.

criteria: The essential outcome and unacceptable states are explicit.
Response capability is not reduced to headcount or number of labels.
Attenuating a disturbance is distinguished from suppressing its signal.
A claim is revised when its modelling assumptions change.

title: Transposing theory: move up to a pattern and back down
focus: Test a structural analogy rather than importing a solution because two situations sound alike.
scope: A basic abstraction-and-return rehearsal for the framework's transposing-theory row. Its resource list also cites Yi Lin's systemic yoyo; this exercise does not teach or validate that distinct formal model. The terminology and intended depth should be checked with your tutor.
scenario: Fictional case A: a warehouse orders replacement stock from last month's sales. Delivery takes four weeks. When shelves empty, several managers independently raise urgent orders. Stock later arrives together and exceeds storage capacity. Fictional case B: a council trains additional caseworkers using last quarter's backlog. Training takes six months. Several services independently commission the same small pool of trainers. Trainees arrive after demand has changed. Casework, unlike boxes, also varies in urgency, consent, relationship and complexity.

rounds.task: Write the common structural pattern without using warehouse or council nouns.
rounds.output: A four-part abstract model.
rounds.answer: A demand signal is delayed; a replenishment decision is made from it; the replenishment takes time; independent decision-makers may duplicate orders while the pipeline is invisible. The resulting overshoot is a hypothesis generated by that structure. 'Both organisations need better leadership' is too unspecific to transpose or test.

rounds.task: Map the abstract elements into case B.
rounds.output: A correspondence table with at least one non-correspondence.
rounds.answer: Stock corresponds only partially to available trained capacity; orders correspond to training commissions; delivery lead time to training delay; hidden pipeline to trainees already commissioned. People are not interchangeable inventory. Capabilities, supervision, retention, consent and case mix alter the comparison. State where the analogy stops.

rounds.task: Derive a modest intervention and a falsification test.
rounds.output: One intervention hypothesis with a measurable challenge.
rounds.answer: Make current training commitments and expected completion dates visible across services before commissioning more. Predict fewer duplicated commissions without reducing necessary capability. Compare unique requirements, commissions and later staffing gaps. If duplication persists because services require incompatible skills, the shared-inventory model needs revision rather than stronger enforcement.

checks.q: Which is the transferable part of the example?
options: A warehouse's staffing ratio
The delayed signal, replenishment pipeline and duplicated decisions
The claim that people are stock
checks.explanation: The proposed correspondence concerns relationships and delays. Neither an arbitrary parameter nor a literal identity between people and inventory follows.

checks.q: What should happen when case mix invalidates interchangeability?
options: Discard the evidence to protect the analogy
Revise the abstraction or stop using it
Assume the model applies because it is systemic
checks.explanation: A theory is useful through an explicit fit with the situation. A failed correspondence is information about its limit.

repair.broken: 'Hospitals are factories, so the warehouse rule should be applied unchanged to patients.'
repair.fix: Name the limited structural correspondence, then examine consent, urgency, variable needs, clinical judgement and care relationships. Transfer a question or tested mechanism, not a whole identity or managerial prescription.

retry.task: Apply the same pattern to recruiting volunteer interpreters. Name one correspondence and one reason a numerical inventory rule might fail.
retry.answer: A recruitment-to-availability delay is a correspondence. Language combinations, availability, confidentiality and matching requirements make volunteer capacity heterogeneous. A single total may hide a shortage in one language alongside unused capacity in another.

criteria: The abstract pattern contains relationships, not just similar vocabulary.
Correspondences and non-correspondences are both recorded.
A practical prediction could be challenged by evidence.
The learner returns to and revises the original situation.

title: Soft Systems Methodology: build a model that follows its purpose
focus: Move from a messy situation through purposeful perspectives to a logically defensible activity model and comparison.
scope: A compact SSM rehearsal. The stages organise learning here; they are not a claim that SSM is a mandatory linear project sequence. An activity model is an inquiry device, not a description of what the organisation really is.
scenario: Fictional case: a repair cooperative allocates home-repair visits. Its scheduler wants every technician hour booked. Residents want a usable home and predictable appointments. Technicians want the information and parts needed to finish safely. The funder pays for completed visits, even when another visit is needed. Residents with uncertain work shifts often miss appointments. The cooperative's board can change booking rules but cannot compel a resident to be at home. There is no evidence yet about which change would improve completed repairs.

rounds.task: Make a rich picture of the situation.
rounds.output: One picture or accessible narrative showing the competing concerns.
rounds.answer: Include residents, technicians, scheduler, funder and board; show funding for visits, information and parts, uncertain shifts, missed appointments and conflicting meanings of success. Show tensions and absences, not only a flowchart. A resident's absence is an event to understand, not proof of irresponsibility.

rounds.task: Write two relevant root definitions using PQR.
rounds.output: Two distinct purposeful perspectives, each one sentence.
rounds.answer: Resident perspective: 'Enable agreed safe repairs to be completed, by coordinating access, diagnosis, parts and work with residents, in order to restore a usable home with manageable disruption.' Scheduling perspective: 'Allocate available technician time, by matching eligible jobs to slots and skills, in order to use the cooperative's funded capacity.' Neither is declared the true purpose. The difference is useful for inquiry.

rounds.task: Check the resident definition with CATWOE.
rounds.output: Six explicit entries, including the transformation.
rounds.answer: Customers: residents benefiting or suffering, including those excluded by booking rules. Actors: residents, booking staff, technicians and suppliers carrying out the activities. Transformation: an agreed repair need becomes a completed, checked repair, not simply a person becoming 'a customer'. Weltanschauung: restoring a usable home justifies organising around completion and disruption. Owner: the board can stop or change the cooperative's arrangement; residents also control access. Environment: safety obligations, available skills, supply times and constraints outside this model's control. Do not put the proposed new booking rule in Environment merely because it exists today.

rounds.task: Build the minimum activity model for the resident definition.
rounds.output: Five to nine verb-led activities with dependencies and monitoring.
rounds.answer: A defensible model is: agree the repair need; establish access constraints; diagnose work and materials; arrange a feasible visit; perform the repair; check completion with the resident; monitor performance and revise arrangements. 'Arrange a feasible visit' depends on access and diagnosis; performance review receives evidence from completion checking. Assess efficacy (did the repair occur?), efficiency (what resources and effort did it use?) and effectiveness (does it contribute to the longer-term purpose?). These are logical requirements of this definition, not a copy of departments.

rounds.task: Compare the model with the case and propose one accommodation.
rounds.output: A three-row comparison and a feasible next inquiry.
rounds.answer: For 'check completion', the case reports paid visits but not resident-verified completion: investigate the gap. For 'establish access', uncertain shifts are known but the booking response is not: ask residents. For 'monitor', the funder's measure may conflict with completion: discuss a paired completion measure. A possible accommodation is to retain visit reporting while jointly trialling resident-confirmed completion and flexible scheduling. It needs consent and negotiation; a neat model does not establish agreement.

checks.q: Which transformation matches the resident root definition?
options: Unallocated slots become allocated slots
Agreed repair needs become completed, checked repairs
Residents become compliant
checks.explanation: The transformation must follow the selected purpose. Slot allocation belongs to the other root definition; compliance changes the purpose without acknowledging it.

checks.q: What is wrong with activity boxes labelled Board, Finance and Technician?
options: They are roles or units, not logically required activities
They are always outside the system
Nothing: any organisation chart is an activity model
checks.explanation: Use verbs describing necessary activities. Roles may perform them, but a departmental chart does not establish the activity logic.

checks.q: A model differs from current practice. What follows?
options: Current practice must immediately copy the model
The difference supplies a question for structured comparison
The model is necessarily false
checks.explanation: SSM uses the comparison for learning and debate. The model is purposeful and selective; the difference does not by itself command a redesign or invalidate the inquiry.

repair.broken: Root definition: restore usable homes. Model: maximise visits, close tickets, penalise missed appointments. No completion check.
repair.fix: The model has silently substituted the funder's or scheduler's purpose. Either label it as another purposeful model or rebuild it around agreed needs, completion and resident experience. Add monitoring that can challenge the arrangement, not merely count its transactions.

retry.task: The board now insists on minimising disruption rather than maximising technician utilisation. Add one necessary activity and one comparison question.
retry.answer: An explicit activity could be 'agree acceptable timing and disruption with the resident'. Ask whether current booking captures and honours those constraints. Other activities are acceptable when logically derived and not simply desirable extras. Record the unresolved trade-off with capacity rather than assuming it disappears.

criteria: At least two purposes remain distinguishable.
CATWOE supports rather than replaces a coherent root definition.
Activities logically follow the selected purpose and include monitoring.
Comparison produces inquiry and possible accommodation, not a claim that the model is reality.

title: System Dynamics: build, calculate and challenge a queue model
focus: Distinguish causal-loop reasoning from an executable stock-flow model and verify a small model by hand.
scope: An original discrete-time stock-flow rehearsal with a deliberately simple boundary. It is not a prediction of a real service and does not validate a model merely because it runs.
scenario: Fictional case: a service starts week 1 with a backlog of 40 cases. Exactly 12 new cases arrive at the start of each week. Staff can complete at most 10 cases per week in weeks 1 and 2. Additional trained capacity is available from the start of week 3, raising the limit to 16. All cases are identical in this toy model. Completions during a week cannot exceed that week's starting backlog plus arrivals. There are no withdrawals or reopens in the first model.

rounds.task: Draw the stock-flow structure and state its units.
rounds.output: One stock, two flows and an explicit time step.
rounds.answer: Stock: backlog in cases. Inflow: arrivals in cases/week. Outflow: completions in cases/week. Capacity is a limit on the outflow, not another stock of cases. For a one-week step: end backlog = start backlog + arrivals - completions; completions = min(capacity, start backlog + arrivals). The minimum prevents negative backlog. Changing the time step would require rates and event timing to be handled consistently.

rounds.task: Calculate the first four end-of-week backlogs.
rounds.output: A four-row calculation table.
rounds.answer: Week 1: 40 + 12 - 10 = 42. Week 2: 42 + 12 - 10 = 44. Week 3: 44 + 12 - 16 = 40. Week 4: 40 + 12 - 16 = 36. Backlog rises before the extra capacity arrives, then falls by four cases per week while enough cases remain. A drop in arrivals is not needed to explain this change.

rounds.task: Describe a balancing feedback that could generate the capacity decision.
rounds.output: A signed loop and its delay.
rounds.answer: Backlog (+) increases perceived capacity gap; gap (+) increases training commissions; commissions (+), after a training delay, increase effective completion capacity; capacity (+) increases completions; completions (-) reduce backlog. The single negative causal link makes this proposed loop balancing. The fixed capacity schedule in the numerical exercise is externally specified: the loop is not yet implemented in its equations. Do not claim a two-flow stock model already simulates the decision feedback.

rounds.task: Run two extreme-condition checks.
rounds.output: Results for zero arrivals and for an almost empty queue.
rounds.answer: With zero arrivals and backlog 40, capacity 10 yields backlog 30 after one week. With starting backlog 2, arrivals 0 and capacity 16, completions are 2 and ending backlog 0, not -14. These are necessary accounting checks, not evidence that the real service behaves like the model.

rounds.task: Identify a missing mechanism that could reverse the policy conclusion.
rounds.output: One boundary extension and data needed to assess it.
rounds.answer: Rushed work might reopen cases, making nominal completions overstate resolved need. Add a reopen inflow with an explicit timing rule and measure its rate. Alternatively, training may temporarily reduce experienced staff availability. A model boundary that omits these effects may overstate the improvement from additional capacity.

checks.q: What is the backlog at the end of week 2?
options: 20 cases
44 cases
64 cases
checks.explanation: The backlog gains 12-10=2 cases in each of two weeks: 40+2+2=44. Capacity is a rate of completion, not the number left waiting.

checks.q: Which unit belongs to the backlog?
options: Cases/week
Cases
Weeks/case
checks.explanation: Backlog accumulates cases. A flow has cases/week, and a processing time may have weeks/case under a specified interpretation.

checks.q: Does a positive link mean a beneficial effect?
options: Yes
No: it means change in the same direction, other influences held constant
Only for reinforcing loops
checks.explanation: Polarity describes a causal direction, not desirability. A reinforcing loop can amplify either improvement or deterioration.

checks.q: Starting backlog 2, zero arrivals, capacity 16: how many cases complete?
checks.explanation: The outflow is limited by available cases. A negative backlog is an accounting defect, not an innovative service model.

repair.broken: Backlog = arrivals / completions. It is labelled 'cases', and managers say its fall proves a balancing feedback loop.
repair.fix: The ratio of two rates is dimensionless and is not an accumulation. Use the stock accounting equation with an initial condition. A changing ratio does not identify a closed causal mechanism. State and test the decision rules and delays separately.

retry.task: From week 3, let 25% of each week's 16 completions return as new backlog at the end of that same week. Calculate end backlogs for weeks 3 and 4.
retry.answer: Each week four cases reopen. Week 3 ends at 44+12-16+4=44; week 4 also ends at 44. Gross completion capacity increased but net resolution is only 12 cases/week. This timing is stipulated for the exercise; a real reopen delay must be investigated rather than assumed.

criteria: Stocks, rates, units, initial conditions and timing are explicit.
The four baseline calculations and empty-queue test are correct.
Loop polarity is causal rather than moral.
The numerical model is distinguished from an unimplemented feedback hypothesis.
A missing mechanism and a way to test it are named.

title: Viable System Model: diagnose functions and channels
focus: Choose a recursion, identify operational units, and test management functions without turning the VSM into an organisation chart.
scope: A basic organisational diagnosis. Functions can be distributed or combined in people and groups. The exercise does not establish that every multi-agency network has a single legitimate metasystem.
scenario: Fictional case: Neighbourhood Advice Cooperative runs North, Central and South advice centres. Each serves local residents, organises its own advisers and decides ordinary cases. They share specialist interpreters and sometimes double-book them. A cooperative operations group negotiates budgets and capacity with centre leads. A quality reviewer periodically observes cases directly, with an agreed learning remit. A small planning group studies changing resident needs and technology, but its reports rarely reach operations. The elected board sets identity and purpose and settles major policy disputes. An urgent safeguarding concern currently travels through three monthly reporting meetings.

rounds.task: State the focal system and one level above and below it.
rounds.output: A recursion statement and three candidate operational units.
rounds.answer: Focal system: the advice cooperative as a whole. Candidate System 1 units: the three centres, each with an operation, local management and a relevant environment. Within a centre, case teams may form the next level if they genuinely carry primary activity with appropriate management. A wider partnership is only a candidate level above: do not assert that it governs the cooperative without evidence and legitimacy.

rounds.task: Map the case evidence to Systems 1-5 and 3*.
rounds.output: A function-evidence table, leaving unknowns visible.
rounds.answer: System 1: centres delivering advice in their local environments. System 2: arrangements damping interference between centres, such as interpreter booking protocols; the double-booking suggests a gap. System 3: the operations group's resource bargains, synergy and internal regulation. System 3*: the agreed direct sampling of operational reality, distinct from routine reports. System 4: the planning group's outside-and-future intelligence. System 5: identity, policy and balancing present and future through the elected board. These are functions evidenced by activities, not job titles.

rounds.task: Diagnose two channel failures.
rounds.output: Two hypotheses, each with a verification question.
rounds.answer: The System 3/4 dialogue may be weak: ask how a recent external change altered an operational decision, and how operational experience revised a future proposal. Urgent safeguarding signals are too slow for their purpose: trace a concern's actual escalation and response time. A System 2 booking weakness is another defensible hypothesis. A missing line in your diagram alone is not proof that the function is absent.

rounds.task: Design a correction that preserves local autonomy.
rounds.output: One bounded change and a check for over-centralisation.
rounds.answer: Give centres a shared interpreter availability view and agreed conflict-resolution protocol, while leaving normal case decisions local. Establish a direct urgent escalation route with named response responsibility. For future adaptation, create a recurring 3/4 conversation using both demand evidence and operational constraints. Check whether the new arrangement removes local discretion that does not need to be centralised.

rounds.task: Test the diagnosis with operational evidence.
rounds.output: A short sampling plan.
rounds.answer: Trace an ordinary case, a cross-centre resource conflict, a future-driven change and an urgent exception. Ask the people doing the work how information and authority actually move. Distinguish formal policy from observed practice. Use direct observation with a legitimate remit, not covert inspection presented as neutral learning.

checks.q: Which is the strongest System 2 example in this case?
options: A shared interpreter scheduling protocol
The elected board's identity statement
A future-demand study
checks.explanation: The protocol reduces interference among operational units. Identity is a System 5 concern; outside-and-future intelligence is System 4.

checks.q: What distinguishes System 3* from routine System 3 reports?
options: It is a more senior manager
It provides a direct, agreed check on operational reality
It is every financial audit, regardless of purpose
checks.explanation: The distinction is the information channel and function, not rank or the word 'audit'. Its remit and effect on trust still matter.

checks.q: Must the three centres have identical local arrangements to be System 1 units?
options: Yes
No, they need viable local responses within the cooperative's identity and constraints
Only if the chart is symmetrical
checks.explanation: Different environments may require different response variety. Coherence does not require identical local operations.

repair.broken: The chief executive is labelled S5, all middle managers S2, every worker S1, and the outside world is omitted.
repair.fix: Choose the recursion and primary activities first. Identify actual functions, environments and channels. One person may perform several functions; a worker may exercise local intelligence and policy. An organisational rank is not a VSM system number.

retry.task: An autonomous helpline is added with its own users, case decisions and local management. Is it necessarily System 2 because it connects centres?
retry.answer: No. It may be another System 1 unit if advice delivery is a primary activity at the chosen recursion. Some of its activities could also support coordination. Determine function, operational autonomy and environment rather than classifying it by the word 'helpline'.

criteria: The recursion and system of interest are explicit.
Operational units include operation, management and environment.
Systems 2, 3, 3*, 4 and 5 are differentiated by function.
The diagnosis tests channels and evidence, not just missing boxes.
Corrections consider autonomy, legitimacy and timely response.

title: Critical Systems Heuristics: inspect all twelve boundary categories
focus: Build an is/ought boundary critique and show how a change in boundary alters a judgement.
scope: This exercise checks the completeness and consistency of boundary reasoning. It does not supply a morally unique answer or pretend that the practitioner represents every affected person.
scenario: Fictional case: a council proposes replacing its assisted benefits-application desk with a digital service. The finance director sponsors the proposal and counts annual administrative cost as success. A vendor controls the software design. The council controls staffing and opening hours. An analyst advises using completion rates from current online users. People unable to start online are absent from that dataset. A tenants' group has asked to be heard but has no place in the decision meetings. The project document says 'digital by default is modern and fair'. No replacement assistance or appeal route has been agreed.

rounds.task: Complete the four groups of boundary categories in the descriptive 'is' mode.
rounds.output: Twelve labelled entries, separating case evidence from unknowns.
rounds.answer: Motivation: beneficiary, purpose, measure. The sponsor prioritises administrative savings; whether all applicants benefit is unestablished. Control: decision-maker, controlled resources, decision environment. Council staffing decisions and vendor software control differ; applicants' internet access is not simply a project-controlled resource. Knowledge: expert, relevant expertise, guarantor of success. Analyst/vendor knowledge dominates; current online completion is treated as assurance, but excludes non-starters. Legitimacy: witness for affected people, emancipation or opportunity to challenge, and worldview. The tenants' group is not yet represented; an appeal route is absent; 'modern and fair' is a contested framing. Use 'unknown' where the case does not specify a fact.

rounds.task: Write an 'ought' counterpart for each category.
rounds.output: Twelve proposals with the person or group whose judgement they express.
rounds.answer: One defensible account includes all eligible applicants as intended beneficiaries; successful access to entitlement as purpose; cost, completion, exclusion and effort as measures; explicit council accountability and vendor constraints; assisted access resources; knowledge from applicants and frontline staff; assurance through disaggregated evidence and challenge; an independent voice for affected non-participants; accessible contest and redress; and a worldview in which access is not conditional on digital confidence. These are proposals to discuss, not automatically legitimate claims made on others' behalf.

rounds.task: Trace one boundary change into the evaluation.
rounds.output: A before-and-after judgement with a changed evidence requirement.
rounds.answer: If the beneficiary boundary expands from current online users to all eligible applicants, the online completion rate is no longer sufficient. Count failed starts and people using or needing assistance, and ask about effort and exclusion. An apparently cheaper process may transfer cost or prevent access. The new judgement requires evidence; it is not proof that digital service is necessarily bad.

rounds.task: Design a challenge that an affected person can actually use.
rounds.output: One route to contest the proposal without accepting its framing.
rounds.answer: Invite independently supported evidence from people unable to use the digital route, permit oral or assisted submissions, explain how challenges affect the decision, and provide a route to disagree after a meeting. Do not require a person to complete an online consultation to prove that online access is a barrier. Representation and practical ability to challenge are different questions.

checks.q: Does the analyst's involvement resolve the legitimacy questions?
options: Yes: expertise represents everyone
No: expertise and the voice of affected people are different categories
Yes: the data are numerical
checks.explanation: Expertise can inform an inquiry without supplying a witness for affected people or the practical freedom to challenge its assumptions.

checks.q: What does 'ought' mean in this exercise?
options: A hidden fact waiting to be discovered
An explicit normative boundary proposal open to challenge
The tutor's mandatory policy preference
checks.explanation: The task is to make values and boundary choices discussable. A model answer illustrates reasoning, not an authorised settlement of people's interests.

checks.q: Who is missing from the stated online completion measure?
options: Only the vendor
People unable to start the online process
No one, because all applications are digital
checks.explanation: A rate among people already inside the process can exclude those who cannot enter it. The denominator is a boundary decision.

repair.broken: A stakeholder list has twelve names and is labelled 'the twelve CSH questions answered'.
repair.fix: People are not boundary categories. Examine motivation, control, knowledge and legitimacy in both descriptive and normative modes. A single actor may occupy several roles; a crucial role may have no credible representative.

retry.task: The tenants' group gets one seat but cannot alter the agenda or challenge the savings target. Which part of the critique remains open?
retry.answer: Witness or representation may have improved, but emancipation and worldview remain contested. Attendance is not sufficient opportunity to question the terms of the decision. Ask whether dissent can alter evidence, criteria or the decision itself.

criteria: All twelve categories are addressed in both is and ought modes.
Evidence, absence and normative proposals are distinguishable.
An affected voice is not silently replaced by an expert or the practitioner.
A boundary change alters a concrete evaluation or action.
The answer includes a practicable route for challenge.
